# Why is AI-generated language so hard to understand?

**Authors:** Thomas Hikaru Clark Affiliation: New York University Matias B. Martin Affiliation: The University of Texas at Austinthomas.hikaru.clark@nyu.edu {matias.martin,kyle}@utexas.edu Kyle Mahowald Affiliation: The University of Texas at Austinthomas.hikaru.clark@nyu.edu {matias.martin,kyle}@utexas.edu

## Abstract

There is a widespread sense that AI-generated text has recently become harder to understand. In this study, we investigate a set of psycholinguistic features that are known to correlate with human processing difficulty (e.g., object relative clauses, long syntactic dependencies, low-frequency n-grams). Using a novel corpus of AI-generated text across diverse domains, we find that AI models use these difficult features more often than paraphrases generated by round-trip translation. Compared with human writing, all nine frontier and near-frontier models use more inanimate subjects with animate verbs and more low-frequency n-grams, and most also use longer dependencies, more stacked nouns, and more reduced object relatives in conversation; we also demonstrate substantial variation across model families. We propose and test a hypothesis as to why: while human language is optimized for successful communication, AI-generated text is increasingly optimized for other goals like math, code, and reasoning, in which there is a pressure for information density rather than successful communication. We provide a proof-of-concept for this hypothesis by fine-tuning a language model under a length penalty, which leads to a divergence from human-like linguistic behavior. Our findings highlight the axes of misalignment between linguistic processing demands in humans and LLMs, and point toward possible remedies.

## 1 Introduction

Your instinct is right; the convoluted sentence you are currently reading is quietly eating its own reader-patience budget — footnote it. If you saw that sentence in the wild, you might suspect that it’s the product of a modern LLM. It has several linguistic features that are overrepresented in frontier LLM text: an object relative clause, a denominal verb (“footnote”), an inanimate subject used with the verb “eat”, and stacked nouns leading to a low-frequency n-gram sequence (“reader-patience budget”). All of these features are associated with linguistic processing difficulty.

But why would models trained on human text develop linguistic features that hurt intelligibility? And, if they are, is it happening systematically across model families? Here, we study a set of features known to correlate with linguistic processing difficulty and find that they are overrepresented in text generated from recent LLMs, including both closed and open-weight models. We collect a novel corpus of LLM-generated text across diverse domains (chat, coding, essay), and we show that the prevalence of these features, in many models, exceeds that of human-generated reference corpora. Using a round-trip translation paradigm, we further show that these features do not occur in paraphrases that are controlled tightly for semantic content—further evidence they are a result of the specific features of modern post-trained models.

Having established this trend, we then propose and test a hypothesis as to why this pattern may have emerged in LLMs. The psycholinguistics literature shows that human language is largely optimized for communication (Gibson et al., 2019), in the sense of striking an efficient balance between being easy to produce and easy to understand. Empirically, human text is well-optimized relative to random baselines on a number of dimensions, such as minimizing dependency length (Futrell et al., 2015). It follows that models trained to mimic human-generated text should also show a similar profile of linguistic features in their output, but that these patterns may not be preserved in models where communication is not the primary objective, and where humans are largely out of the loop.

Indeed, modern LLMs are not just trained on human-generated text, but undergo extensive post-training for math, coding, and other reasoning tasks. In paradigms like those of Guo et al. (2025), models are rewarded for getting the right answer but not necessarily for clarity. We hypothesize that optimization for these goals, alongside a limit on the context window available to models, leads to information compression in a way that competes with intelligibility. To test that hypothesis, we fine-tune a pre-trained language model under a length penalty, and measure the linguistic profile of its outputs. The model learns to succeed at the task using fewer tokens by leveraging syntactic alternations (cases where there are two ways of expressing the same meaning), even when this makes their linguistic output less humanlike. Furthermore, their preference for information compression bleeds into linguistic alternations that were not seen in training.

In sum, this work tests two specific hypotheses about the intelligibility of AI-generated text. H1: The language output of frontier and near-frontier LLMs overuses linguistic features associated with human comprehension difficulty. H2: A pressure for information density during post-training shifts the language output of LLMs to be less humanlike. Using a combination of linguistic analysis and direct post-training intervention, we find support for both hypotheses. Our findings highlight the dimensions along which human language processing and frontier LLMs are misaligned, and point to possible interventions for addressing this misalignment.

## 2 Background and Related Work

Recent scientific work has attempted to measure the idiosyncrasies of LLMs, such as their tendency to over-use particular words (Juzek and Ward, 2025), or their dense, noun-heavy style Reinhart et al. (2025). These idiosyncrasies may emerge during the post-training process of modern LLMs, including rewards during reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF; Ouyang et al., 2022; Singhal et al., 2024), or reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR; Lambert et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). The distinctive tells of LLM-generated writing have led to AI-generated text detectors (Bao et al., 2024), and have raised questions regarding the impact of such AI-generated writing on linguistic content, with implications for diversity and representation (Padmakumar and He, 2024; Agarwal et al., 2025; Ryan et al., 2024). As a growing share of the text people read is shaped by LLMs, the linguistic properties of AI-generated writing matter not only for detection but also for the human readers who must process it. Yet whether these properties make AI-generated text harder for humans to understand has received little academic attention, despite widespread anecdotal reports of issues with LLM intelligibility (University of Waterloo, 2026).

The field of psycholinguistics has extensively studied the linguistic features that drive comprehension difficulty. Words that are hard to predict are costly to process (Hale, 2001; Levy, 2008), and so are long-distance dependencies, because of limits on memory (Gibson, 1998; Gibson, 2000). Memory-based accounts explain the difficulty of center-embedded sentences (Gibson and Thomas, 1999; Lewis, 1996) and of legalese (Martínez et al., 2022), and temporary ambiguity can derail comprehension in garden-path sentences (Christianson et al., 2001).

Crucially, the human mind operates under distinct pressures and limitations compared with those of LLMs. LLMs are also trained on significantly more data than humans experience during language development Frank (2023). Modern LLMs are able to attend fully to very large context windows (Vaswani et al., 2017; Oh and Linzen, 2026), in contrast with the lossy and distance-sensitive memory of humans (Futrell et al., 2020). Larger LLMs often fit human behavior (e.g., reading times) less well than smaller LLMs (Oh and Schuler, 2023; Oh et al., 2024). Consistent with this pattern, LLMs with artificially constrained memory fit human behavior better (Kuribayashi et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2026; Clark et al., 2025). This suggests that LLMs’ ability to attend fully to long contexts may come at the cost of human-likeness.

Linguistic alternations, in which speakers and writers have multiple options for expressing a given meaning, provide a source of evidence for the preferences guiding human language generation. One purported pressure on human language production is uniform information density (UID) — the idea that speakers spread information evenly across the signal to avoid overloading comprehenders, e.g. by inserting optional words (Levy and Jaeger, 2007; Meister et al., 2021). UID is at odds with maximizing information density, by which shorter members of linguistic alternations would be categorically preferred, and has been proposed as a metric for preference optimization in LLM training to produce more human-aligned text (Li and Xu, 2026). Meanwhile, psycholinguistic evidence also supports a pressure based on cognitive availability during incremental production (Bock, 1987; Clark et al., 2022; Futrell, 2024). Pre-trained LLMs inherit these signatures from their human training text, but post-training for specific tasks (e.g. math, code) may favor information-dense constructions over those that ease human processing or resemble humans.

## 3 Experiment 1: Linguistic features in AI-generated conversations

### 3.1 Linguistic features of interest

The purpose of Experiment 1 is to test H1: do frontier and near-frontier LLMs disproportionately use linguistic features that are linked to human processing difficulty? For each feature, we justify its association with processing difficulty, and explain why it might plausibly arise from a pressure toward information density. Example sentences for each feature are given in Table 2. All features are identified from spaCy dependency parses (Honnibal et al., 2020); for denominal verbs and inanimate subjects, parser-generated candidates are then judged by an automated classifier (Section B.1).

#### N-gram statistics

Predictable words are associated with lower processing difficulty, as measured by reading times (Levy, 2008; Smith and Levy, 2013). From an information-theoretic perspective, a word with a very high n-gram probability is more redundant than one with a low n-gram probability. For a system designed to maximize information density, we might expect high-probability n-grams to be reduced (i.e. common, uninformative, and predictable words being skipped), and higher overall n-gram perplexity (when measured by an independent language model). Against a reference corpus, we measure the rate of unattested pairs, bigrams that never occur in it, and perplexity under a trigram model (Section B.2).

#### Dependency length

Words in a sentence relate to each other via syntactic dependency relations (e.g., between a noun and any determiners or adjectives that modify it, or between a verb and its subject, object, and adverbial modifiers). Long-distance dependencies are known to be difficult to process for humans, due to the additional strain they place on working memory (Gibson, 1998; Gibson, 2000; Grodner and Gibson, 2005), and speakers tend to avoid them (Futrell et al., 2015; Temperley and Gildea, 2018). We standardize dependency length across sentence lengths, as described in Appendix B.

#### Object relative clauses

We measure the rate of object relative clauses (ORCs) in the language output of LLMs, differentiating between ORCs with an overt relativizer (most often that or which) and without one. ORCs are known to present additional processing difficulty compared to subject relative clauses, potentially due to their non-canonical word order and longer dependencies (Staub, 2010), although animacy and frequency reduce the gap (Mak et al., 2006; Reali and Christiansen, 2007). Under the hypothesis that LLMs tend to choose more compressed realizations of a given meaning, we predict object relative clauses will be over-represented, because they tend to replace a (longer) passive construction (The house that the contractors built vs. The house that was built by the contractors), and second, that reduced relative clauses (without the optional relativizer) would be over-represented, because they avoid an optional word.

#### Stacked noun compounds

In English, nouns freely modify other nouns in an adjectival way: in the phrase coffee shop, coffee modifies shop, despite usually appearing as a noun. This feature enables stacking multiple nouns into rich compound words which denote highly specific meanings. However, such stacks can introduce bracketing ambiguity, as in the headline Squad Helps Dog Bite Victim (Cooper, 1980), and disrupt reading (Lauer, 1995; Nakov and Hearst, 2005; Staub et al., 2007; Cohen and Staub, 2014). Here, we measure the rate of occurrence of stacked noun compounds, defined as three or more nouns in a modifier relationship.

#### Denominal verbs

Verbs which are formed directly from nouns, such as in the phrase bottle the whiskey are known as denominal verbs. While some denominal verbs are highly conventionalized and well-attested in human language, using a denominal verb in an ad-hoc way is marked (e.g., calendar it). Readers can interpret such innovations (Clark and Clark, 1979), but part-of-speech conversion triggers syntactic re-evaluation (Thierry et al., 2008), and noun/verb-ambiguous words are processed differently from unambiguous ones (Frazier and Rayner, 1987; Federmeier et al., 2000). Often, the alternative to using a denominal verb is to use a longer, more syntactically complex phrase, e.g. put the whiskey in a bottle. We therefore predict that a pressure for information compression will favor usage of denominal verbs beyond their base rate in humans, even at the expense of intelligibility.

#### Inanimate subjects

We count the instances of inanimate subjects used with active verbs that typically take only animate subjects. Examples include “is_file() swallows that and returns False” and “Puzzle patterns where this asymmetry bites”. Such sentences violate a selectional restriction (Chomsky, 1965) on which verbs typically take which subjects. They can be understood as personification or metonymy (Lakoff and Johnson, 1980), but readers use animacy as a cue during parsing (Trueswell et al., 1994), and without additional context, a mismatch may elicit a P600 response associated with reanalysis (Kim and Osterhout, 2005; Kuperberg, 2007). However, rephrasing these sentences to avoid inanimate subjects would potentially require lengthening the sentence: for example, the word “bites” stands in for “causes an issue”. We speculate that during training, models may have converged to using such constructions as efficient, albeit non-standard, ways of expressing meaning which would otherwise take up more tokens.

### 3.2 Data collection

We collect a corpus of AI-generated conversations (Figure 1) using a set of 14 frontier and non-frontier LLMs: Kimi K2.5, GLM 5, Claude (Sonnet 5, Opus 5, Opus 5.5, Fable 5), and GPT-5.6 (Luna, Terra, Sol), Olmo (Team Olmo et al., 2025) (Base, Instruct, Think), and Llama (Grattafiori et al., 2024) (Base, Instruct). We use a total of 15 conversational starting prompts, or seeds, consisting of 10 chat seeds and 5 coding seeds. Each coding seed involves a request to clone a real, public GitHub repo, identify bugs, and implement fixes within a sandbox environment. Chat sessions were capped at 12 turns (a simulated human query and a model response) and coding sessions at 11 turns plus a fixed closing message. In a third setting, each model writes single-turn essays to seven PERSUADE 2.0 assignments. Full data collection procedures and API costs are described in Appendix A.

### 3.3 Comparison to human baselines

Where available, we compute a human baseline for the linguistic feature of interest, on approximately genre-matched text: OpenSubtitles (Lison and Tiedemann, 2016) for chat, StackExchange for coding, and student essays from the PERSUADE 2.0 corpus (Crossley et al., 2024) for essays. We additionally include a Wikipedia comparison. The same corpora serve as the references for the n-gram measures (Section B.2).

### 3.4 Round-trip translation

We employ round-trip translation (bilingual pivoting), an established paraphrasing method that preserves meaning at scale Bannard and Callison-Burch (2005); Mallinson et al. (2017); Wieting and Gimpel (2018); Federmann et al. (2019), as a method for separating a model output’s characteristic syntactic profile from its semantics. Translation normalizes the output to frequent forms, reducing lexical and syntactical richness Vanmassenhove et al. (2019); Vanmassenhove et al. (2021) and stripping stylistic and authorial traits Rabinovich et al. (2017); Prabhumoye et al. (2018). The result is a parallel corpus in which each translation is paired with its source sentence. Because the round trip holds the semantic content of each response fixed while replacing its wording, a feature that becomes less frequent after the round trip is one that the model chose over an available alternative way of expressing the same content. To create this parallel corpus, we translate each sentence independently from English to Japanese and back with NLLB-200 (3.3B; NLLB Team, 2024). Japanese was chosen because pivot languages unrelated to English tend to yield more diverse paraphrases Federmann et al. (2019).

### 3.5 Results: AI models overuse constructions with known processing costs

Figure 5 compares the linguistic features of interest across the three settings of Chat, Code, and Essay, and 14 LLMs (12 in chat, 9 in coding, and all 14 in essays). Figure 6 compares the LLM-generated corpus to the parallel corpus derived via round-trip translation. We highlight several results.

#### Frontier models over-use rare n-grams, denominal verbs, inanimate subjects, and reduced ORCs, relative to the paraphrase distribution.

Across all three settings and almost all frontier and near-frontier models, the round-trip translations reveal that AI text has more unattested bigrams and higher n-gram perplexity. These effects are absent or small for the Llama models and the Olmo base model, but Olmo Think shows effects as large as those of the frontier models. Within the Olmo family, the effects grow from the base to the instruct to the reasoning model. The same pattern largely holds for denominal verbs and inanimate subjects, as well as for ORCs with no relativizer. Meanwhile, models under-use ORCs with the relativizer, suggesting a preference for skipping optional words (Figure 4). Similar patterns hold for stacked nouns and dependency length in chat and coding. In the essays, dependency length is unchanged or slightly longer after the round trip, and stacked nouns change significantly for only two models.

#### These effects are smaller overall for the PERSUADE essays.

The PERSUADE essays show smaller changes under round-trip translation on several categories (n-gram measures, dependency lengths, stacked nouns, denominal verbs) relative to chat and coding (Figures 6 and 3(a)). We hypothesize that this is because they involve a single prompt, unlike the many iterated turns of chat and coding. We speculate that certain patterns may emerge in long back-and-forth conversations (which may demand more information compression).

#### There are notable differences between models.

The Llama models and the Olmo base and instruct models change least under round-trip translation (Figure 2) and are closest to the student essays on the n-gram and verb measures. Meanwhile, Olmo Think patterns with the frontier models. Notably, Claude Opus 5.5 is lower than its predecessor Opus 5 on nearly every difficulty-linked measure in every setting (19 of 21 comparisons), with non-overlapping 95% intervals in eight. In sum, most frontier models over-represent linguistically difficult features relative to paraphrases, and relative to human text for inanimate subjects and low-frequency n-grams (Figure 3(b)).

## 4 Experiment 2: Effect of length penalties on language preferences

The purpose of Experiment 2 is to test H2 – the hypothesis that models trained under a pressure for information density are more likely to shift their linguistic output toward difficult and non-humanlike linguistic features. While Experiment 1 provides circumstantial evidence for H2 (e.g., that models over-use constructions that are less verbose than semantically equivalent alternatives), we additionally aim to understand a possible mechanism by which a pressure for information density may arise in LLMs.

### 4.1 Setup

We start with an open-weights model, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2024), and a task of converting JSON-style structured event descriptions into English sentences. We apply fine-tuning via reinforcement learning with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), varying two key parameters: $\beta$ , the KL divergence regularization term which penalizes a model for drifting from the base model’s next-token distribution, and $\lambda$ , a length penalty term which penalizes responses for verbosity. Each event seen during training or testing can be expressed using either member of a syntactic alternation where one alternative is shorter by a known number of tokens (except the particle control, where both orders have the same length). Human speakers use both members of such alternations and choose between them according to context; for example, they are more likely to include an optional that when the material that follows is less predictable (Levy and Jaeger, 2007; Jaeger, 2010). The key question is whether training a model with a length penalty pushes it instead toward a categorical preference for the shorter member, regardless of context, which would be a divergence from human language use. We evaluate in three settings. The trained alternations are new sentences, never seen in training, built from the four alternations used in training. Near transfer denotes test sentences which contain alternations involving the optional word “that” (sure (that), so (that)); however, these specific constructions were not seen during training, so the model omitting “that” in these cases would indicate a generalization to a novel context. Finally, far transfer denotes unrelated alternations (genitive, quantifier, passive and purpose-clause alternations; Table 3), where a model could in theory choose to conserve tokens by choosing the shorter alternation, though this would indicate that the model has generalized to an information-dense preference in contexts unrelated to the training data. See Appendix C for details (Figure 8; Table 4).

### 4.2 Results: A length penalty shifts models toward shorter variants, including in untrained constructions

As can be seen in Figure 7, the probability of using the shorter construction increases as a function of the length penalty $\lambda$ , both with and without the KL penalty $\beta$ . For the setting without KL-regularization, preference for the short alternative rises rapidly as a function of length penalty ( $\lambda$ ). Preference for the short alternation rises, albeit more gradually, even in the presence of KL-regularization. Without KL regularization, runs with $\lambda=0$ had different preferences for the short alternative ranging from 0% to 100% depending on seed, indicating no stable preference. Meanwhile, for any $\lambda>0$ , all seeds converged to a categorical preference for the short alternative. The models learn a tendency for information compression that transfers to additional constructions not seen in training. This was consistent in the near transfer case; far transfer was only observed without KL penalty in the genitive alternation, one of four far-transfer alternations tested (Appendix C).

### 4.3 Discussion

We take these results as a proof of concept that a length penalty used during reinforcement learning with GRPO can directly affect grammatical features. We note that the model was not directly instructed to use compressed or dense language, and was not directly given information about the availability of syntactic alternations. Rather, the penalty resulted in an emergent preference for shorter members of syntactic alternations. Without KL regularization this preference was near-categorical (over 98% short for both trained “that” alternations at every $\lambda>0$ ), unlike human speakers, who choose between the variants by context. Crucially, the models were still able to succeed at their task, since both members of an alternation were valid solutions to the training task. We speculate that the use of verifiable rewards creates an environment where correctness is decoupled from humanlike communication, leading models to converge toward a novel, potentially less comprehensible distribution of language use.

## 5 General Discussion

#### Model Development

Past work has identified RLHF as a potential factor in the rise of word overuse by AI (Juzek and Ward, 2025; Juzek and Ward, 2026). At the same time, a movement from RLHF to RLVR removes humans from the loop, and rewards models for verifiable solutions to problems. Human-feedback training has in fact been found to reward longer outputs (Singhal et al., 2024), so the pressure toward compression that we describe is more plausibly tied to verifiable-reward training. The move away from human feedback removes the implicit pressure for successful communication, and we speculate that this allows LLM-generated language to converge toward a dialect that is useful for LLMs to compress information densely and solve complex problems, but is suboptimal from the perspective of human intelligibility. It is of course also possible to reward models for effective communication; indeed, our results indicate that more recent model variants like Opus 5.5 yield a quantifiable improvement over older models like Opus 5.

#### Implications for psycholinguistics

Multiple threads of research have studied the pressures that have shaped the structure of languages’ grammars and lexicons over the course of language evolution. Various pressures have been identified, such as those for dependency length minimization (Gildea and Temperley, 2010; Temperley and Gildea, 2018), communicative efficiency (Hahn et al., 2020), and uniform information density (Clark et al., 2023). These pressures are not necessarily absolute (i.e. holding in all contexts in all languages), but are supported by large-scale, aggregate evidence across many of the world’s languages. A key takeaway of this literature is that actual human language use is constrained by the realities and limitations of human comprehension, such as lossy working memory or incremental processing; sentences which consistently fail to lead to communicative success are likely to be weeded out from a language via grammar or convention. The wide-scale training and deployment of AI models in contexts where human comprehension is not the primary purpose – such as developing large code bases or solving mathematical problems – presents a fundamentally different set of evolutionary pressures upon the linguistic profile of AI-generated language compared to natural language, and potentially provides novel opportunities for studying the emergence of communication systems.

## 6 Conclusion

For frontier LLMs, the training objectives that make them successful at tasks like agentic coding and mathematical reasoning, especially with long and expensive context windows, are not guaranteed to be aligned with the same pressures that influence human language. Natural language is subject to a pressure for communicative success, assuming the cognitive resource constraints of the human mind and incremental processing. This discrepancy may help explain why many frontier LLMs use linguistic constructions which are technically allowed by the grammar of English, yet are out-of-distribution for human language and are associated with comprehension difficulty. While increased exposure to LLM-generated text may acclimate humans to these out-of-distribution constructions, many of the patterns that have been evaluated in this work present fundamental challenges to intelligibility, and future work on LLMs may consider methods for better aligning LLM outputs with the needs of human comprehenders, in the service of user experience and monitorability.

## 7 Limitations

We only examine a subset of commonly used models, only conduct analyses in English, and use a limited number of conversation seeds (chat topics and code repositories). Ideally, the study would be replicated on a larger number of seeds and model families. Causally identifying sources of linguistic difficulty in frontier models would ideally involve studying them as they are post-trained, but this is not feasible to do at scale and so we rely on proxies. Similarly, limited compute makes studying post-training difficult.

## Appendix A Data collection protocol details

We collected three sets of model text: multi-turn conversations with a simulated user (chat), multi-turn agentic coding sessions with a simulated repository owner (code), and single-reply persuasive essays written to the assignments of the PERSUADE 2.0 corpus (essay). All three were collected with one harness, described first. Subsequent sections describe what is specific to each setting, the processing applied to the collected text, and the API cost.

### A.1 Common infrastructure

#### Models and access.

A total of 14 models were used, including four closed models from Anthropic (Claude Sonnet 5, Opus 5, Opus 5.5, and Fable 5), three from OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 family (Luna, Terra, and Sol), two open-weight near-frontier models (GLM-5 from Z.ai and Kimi K2.5 from Moonshot AI), and five smaller open models at different stages of training: Llama 3.1 8B (base and Instruct) and Olmo 3 7B (base, Instruct, and Think). The nine frontier or near-frontier models were called through Amazon Bedrock (region us-east-1) on the API endpoint that Bedrock serves for each family: the Converse API for the Claude models, the OpenAI Responses API for the GPT models, and the OpenAI-compatible chat completions API for GLM and Kimi. The smaller open models were run locally on an Apple M4 Max with mlx-lm 0.32.0, from 8-bit quantized weights. The simulated user in the chat and code settings is Claude Sonnet 4.6 (not one of the nine studied frontier models), called through Bedrock.

#### Agent harness.

Every call to a chat-trained model, including the simulated user’s, goes through Pi (@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent, pinned to version 0.84.4), an open-source agent harness. The two base models cannot be driven through a chat interface and were called directly on a text-completion endpoint (Section A.4). We chose Pi so that all models run under the same scaffold and the same prompt text rather than under each vendor’s own product. The harness starts one Pi process per conversational turn and resumes the same Pi session on each later turn. Each run has its own freshly generated Pi configuration directory; Pi’s extensions, skills, prompt templates and context files (such as a repository’s AGENTS.md) are switched off, as are its context compaction and its own retry logic.

#### Generation settings.

For the nine non-local models, each model ran at its provider’s defaults. The maximum output length is 32,000 tokens per call (Kimi K2.5 is served with a 16,384-token ceiling by its provider; no reply approached either limit). Reasoning is requested at Pi’s “medium” level, mapped to each model’s corresponding level: adaptive thinking for the Claude models and medium reasoning effort for the GPT models, GLM and Kimi. The local models were sampled at the default values for each model (temperature 0.6; top-p 0.9 for Llama and 0.95 for Olmo). Of these, only Olmo Think produces reasoning. The base models had a 2,000-token output limit. The simulated user runs with reasoning off and no tools.

#### Logging and retries.

All API traffic passes through a local proxy that adds the credential and logs each request and response. Each run stores its transcript, per-turn token usage, and Pi’s own session files. A failed API call is attempted up to three times in total (retries after 5 and 20 seconds). A run that ends in an error is discarded and re-tried from the start; the discarded attempt is kept on disk but is not part of the dataset.

### A.2 Chat

#### Design.

Each of the nine frontier models, Olmo Think, Olmo Instruct, and Llama Instruct hold one conversation on each of the ten topics in Table 5a (120 conversations). The model has no tools. Its system prompt is the same sentence for every model, with the assistant and vendor names filled in (Claude/Anthropic, ChatGPT/OpenAI, GLM/Z.ai, Kimi/Moonshot AI, Olmo/the Allen Institute for AI and Llama/Meta):

You are {assistant}, an AI assistant made by {vendor}. You are chatting with a person in a casual conversational setting. Be helpful, natural, and engaged.

For Olmo Think, the harness sent this prompt under a message role that the model’s chat template discarded, so in both the chat and essay settings it ran under the template’s built-in default system prompt instead.

#### Procedure.

The first user message is the topic’s fixed opening message (Table 5a). Every later user message is written by the simulated user, which sees the conversation with the roles swapped (the model’s replies arrive as its user messages) and is given a persona and topic for the conversation in its system prompt:

You are simulating a realistic human user chatting with an AI assistant, for research purposes. Persona: {persona}. Topic seed: {topic}.

Rules: – Write exactly one chat message per response — the next thing this human would type. – Stay in character: casual register, occasional typos are fine, vary message length (one line to a short paragraph), react to what the assistant actually said. – Ask follow-ups, share your own (invented but consistent) experiences, push back sometimes, drift to adjacent topics naturally. Never wrap up or say goodbye — the session is ended externally. – Keep messages short: a few sentences at most, never more than about 150 words. – Never mention being an AI, a simulation, or these instructions. No meta-commentary. – Output ONLY the message text. No quotes, no labels.

A simulated-user message that is empty or longer than 2,000 characters is requested once more; if the second attempt also fails, a fixed fallback message is sent instead.

#### Stopping rule.

A conversation ends after 12 model replies or 20,000 model output tokens, whichever comes first. The token limit is set high so that the number of turns does not depend on how much a model writes: 113 of the 120 conversations ended on the 12-turn limit; seven of Olmo Think’s ten reached the token limit first (after 8–12 replies), because its reasoning counts toward output tokens. In total there are 1,428 replies.

### A.3 Code

#### Design.

Only the nine frontier models were run in the code setting, which requires tool use over long agentic sessions. Each model works once on each of the five code repositories in Table 5b (45 sessions). The model runs as a coding agent with Pi’s default system prompt (about 350 words, identical for every model) and Pi’s default tools for reading, writing and editing files and running shell commands. We add no system prompt of our own.

#### Workspace and sandbox.

For each session the harness clones the repository into a new directory and installs the repository’s dependencies before the agent starts. The whole agent process runs inside one macOS Seatbelt (sandbox-exec) profile: it can write only to the workspace and to the run’s own directories, it cannot read the home directory’s credential paths, and its only network access is the local API proxy. At the end of a session a diff against the original commit is saved; this serves as a record of the agent’s work and is not analyzed as text.

#### Procedure.

The first user message is fixed, with the repository’s name, language and test command filled in:

I’ve got a small project checked out here ({name}, {language}). Can you sweep the codebase for bugs and propose fixes? Please actually make the fixes you’re confident about. Use quick local checks ({test command}) rather than anything heavyweight — no deployments, no installing big new dependencies.

One thing: this box has no network access, and the dependencies are already installed in {path}, so nothing needs fetching.

Each user message starts an episode: the model works, with as many tool calls as it chooses, until it returns control. Later user messages come from the same simulated user as in the chat setting, under the same system prompt, with the topic “reviewing an automated bug sweep of {name} ({language}, {domain})” and this persona:

the developer who owns this repository. You know the project’s purpose and history but not the internals of every module — you are not an expert on this code. You ask about specific findings the assistant reports, ask it to explain fixes in plain terms, question changes that look risky, and sometimes ask for one more pass over an area you care about. You write like a working developer in a terminal: brief, concrete, lowercase is fine

The simulated user sees only the text of the conversation: its own messages and the text the model wrote. It does not see tool calls, tool output or diffs.

#### Stopping rule.

A session ends after 11 episodes, or earlier once the session’s episode-final text reaches a cumulative estimated 8,000 tokens; the rule is checked only between episodes. The session then closes with one more fixed user message asking the model to write a summary of its work to a file (MEMORY.md) so that the session could be continued later. The reply to this closing message is collected but left out of the analysis. Of the 45 sessions, 42 ended on the turn limit and three (all Opus 5) on the token limit.

#### Unit of analysis.

In both settings we analyze turn-final replies: the last text the model writes in reply to a user message, with no tool call after it. In chat every reply is turn-final. In code, text written between tool calls is not analyzed, and an episode that ends on a tool call does not contribute a reply.

### A.4 Essay

#### Student essays.

The human comparison is the PERSUADE 2.0 corpus of essays by US students in grades 6–12 (Crossley et al., 2024). We use the corpus’s independent writing assignments only, since the text-dependent assignments rely on source articles not included in the corpus, and we drop essays with a missing grade level, English-language-learner status or score. Seven assignments remained: cell phones at school, community service, distance learning, grades for extracurricular activities, mandatory extracurricular activities, seeking multiple opinions, and summer projects. From these we keep the essays with a holistic score of 5 or 6 on the corpus’s 1–6 scale: 2,934 essays, between 54 and 1,014 per assignment.

#### Model essays.

Each model writes ten essays for each of the seven assignments (980 essays). The system prompt is the first sentence of the chat prompt alone (“You are {assistant}, an AI assistant made by {vendor}.”), without the sentence about a casual conversation. The two base models have no chat interface and were given the assignment as a document to continue: the assignment text, a blank line, and the line “Essay:”. Generation stopped at a second “Essay:” line, the end of text, or 2,000 tokens; 31 of their 140 essays reached that limit. Generation settings are otherwise those of the chat setting. The models are not shown student essays and are not asked to write as a student. All 980 runs completed on the first attempt with no refusals.

### A.5 Processing

#### Chat and code.

Turn-final replies are read from the transcripts. Markup for emphasis and links is removed, but the text inside it is kept. Fenced code blocks, HTML and images are removed. Inline code spans, URLs, file paths, code identifiers and inline mathematics are each replaced by a single placeholder word, so that a sentence containing one still counts as one sentence; n-grams containing the placeholder are not counted. Arrows, emoji and stray mathematical symbols are removed and end the stretch. No sentence or n-gram may cross a heading, list item, table cell or paragraph break. Sentences are split with syntok. The same extraction is applied to the human reference corpora.

#### Essays.

Student and model essays share one cleaning procedure: encoding errors are repaired and quotation marks and whitespace are normalized; up to four leading title, name or date lines are dropped; and each of the corpus’s masked-name placeholders (for example Generic_Name) is replaced by a one-word stand-in name, which is excluded from noun counts and from any n-gram that contains it. Spelling is not corrected. Model essays are first converted from markdown to plain text. In this step, a leading heading is dropped as the title, and text set apart from the essay by a horizontal rule (such as a note to the reader) is removed. Section headings are kept as paragraphs but left out of sentence-level measures. Bracketed slots such as [Your Name] are replaced by the same stand-ins. For three Kimi K2.5 essays, reasoning text that preceded a </think> marker in the reply was also removed.

### A.6 Cost and timeline

The main chat and code collection ran from September 4th to 10th 2026 for eight models; Opus 5.5 was released afterward and was collected under the same protocol on September 24th. The smaller open-weight models (Olmo and Llama families; chat and essays) were collected on October 11th. The frontier models’ essays were collected on September 25th. ## Appendix B Analysis details

### B.1 Feature detection

All text is parsed with spaCy (Honnibal et al., 2020) (en_core_web_trf). Object relatives, stacked nouns and dependency lengths are read from the dependency parse. For denominal verbs and inanimate subjects, the parse supplies candidates: verbs whose lemma is used predominantly as a noun in the setting’s human corpus, and active verbs whose subject is an inanimate noun, a pronoun such as it or this, or a code span. Each candidate is then judged in its sentence by an external classifier (Jev 1.13.011 1 https://typesafe.ai), and we count the candidates it accepts with probability above 0.5.

### B.2 Human baselines and n-gram references

Baselines for OpenSubtitles, StackExchange and Wikipedia are computed on a random sample of about 500,000 words from each. For n-gram statistics, we build one trigram model per reference corpus (modified Kneser–Ney smoothing, built with KenLM; Heafield, 2011) and score chat against OpenSubtitles, coding against StackExchange, and essays against Wikipedia. Unattested pairs are reported per 1,000 pairs. Because the chat and coding references are also the human baselines for those settings, we report no human n-gram baseline there; the student essays are scored against Wikipedia in the same way as the model essays.

### B.3 Dependency length standardization

Dependency length positively correlates with sentence length (the maximum possible dependency length in a sentence is one less than the number of words in the sentence), so models that write longer sentences would score higher even with similar syntactic profiles. To remove this, we use direct standardization (using an analogous method to age-standardization in epidemiology). Each sentence goes into one of five length bins (1–5, 6–10, 11–15, 16–20 and 21–30 words, punctuation not counted), and sentences over 30 words are dropped. Only arcs where neither end is punctuation are counted, and the root is excluded. For each source (i.e. different models, humans), we compute each bin’s mean arc length. To standardize, bin weights are computed using the Wikipedia corpus to generate a ‘standard distribution’ of sentence length: for each bin, its weight is the share of total dependency arcs in Wikipedia which came from sentences in that bin. The standardized value is then the average of the bin means, weighted by the Wikipedia-based weights. In other words, this procedure asks “If each source had the same sentence-length distribution as Wikipedia, how long would dependencies be on average?”

### B.4 Details of Figures 5, 6 and 2

In Figure 5, each diamond is a model’s value pooled over its conversations (10 in chat, 5 in coding) or its 70 essays, and bars are 95% bootstrap intervals from resampling whole conversations (essays within prompt). The shaded band around the student-essay line is its 95% interval. No human line is drawn where the human corpus is itself the n-gram reference (n-gram panels in chat and coding; Wikipedia in essays), or for denominal verbs and inanimate subjects in chat and coding, which were not scored on the human corpora.

In Figure 6, filled diamonds are the original text and open circles the round trip. Stars mark a two-sided paired jackknife $t$ -test of the difference over conversations (essays within prompt), not adjusted for the number of comparisons: * $p<.05$ , ** $p<.01$ , *** $p<.001$ .

In Figure 2, for each measure and setting, the absolute difference between the round-trip and original values is divided by the standard deviation of the original values across models. These are averaged within each of the four measure pairs of Figure 6 and then across pairs. Overall is the mean over the settings in which the model was run.

As a check, we repeated the round-trip procedure with a Russian pivot and with TranslateGemma (4B; Finkelstein et al., 2026) for the nine frontier models. Figure 10 gives words per response for all four combinations of translator and pivot. We maximize the KL-regularized expected reward

$$ \displaystyle J(\theta)={} \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\big[R(x,y)\big] \displaystyle-\beta\,\mathbb{E}_{x}\,\mathrm{KL}\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot|x)\big), $$

where $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is the frozen base model. With LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is the policy network with the adapter disabled. For two variants that tie on task reward and differ by $\Delta$ tokens, the optimum of (1), $\pi^{*}(y|x)\propto\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)\exp(R(x,y)/\beta)$ , satisfies

$$ \log\frac{\pi^{*}(\text{s})}{\pi^{*}(\text{l})}=\log\frac{\pi_{\text{ref}}(\text{s})}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(\text{l})}+\frac{\lambda\Delta}{\beta}, $$

where s and l are the short and long variants. This motivates the choice of $\lambda$ and $\beta$ values. When $\beta=0$ this optimum doesn’t exist, and the shift is limited only by the length of training.

The reward for a completion $y$ to a prompt $x$ is

$$ R(x,y)=c(x,y)\,f(y)-\lambda\,|y|, $$

where $c(x,y)\in\{0,1\}$ is correctness, $f(y)\in\{0,1\}$ is a format check, and $|y|$ is the number of tokens in the completion under the policy’s tokenizer (special tokens not counted). Correctness is rule-based: every argument phrase of the event must appear verbatim (case-insensitive), a dependency parse (spaCy en_core_web_trf) must place each phrase in its role, and the event verb must keep its lemma. Either member of an alternation, and other paraphrases such as passives, are accepted; tense is not checked. The format check requires a single sentence that starts with a capital letter, ends in a period or exclamation mark, and has no preamble, quotation marks or colon.

We use Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; Shao et al., 2024) as implemented in TRL’s GRPOTrainer (TRL 1.13.0). Each optimizer step does the following:

- 1. Sampling. For each of 8 prompts, sample a group of $G=16$ completions from the current policy with vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) (colocated with training) at temperature $T=1.0$ , up to 64 new tokens. That is 128 completions per step.

- 2. Reward. Score each completion with (3).

- 3. Advantage. Group-mean baseline with no standard-deviation scaling (scale_rewards=’none’):

$$ A_{i}=R_{i}-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}R_{j}. $$

(4) The same $A_{i}$ is assigned to every token of completion $i$ . We don’t divide by the group standard deviation because that would change $\lambda$ ’s scale from group to group. In a group where all completions tie on task reward, std scaling would inflate their small length differences to unit scale.

- 4. Loss. loss_type=‘dr_grpo’ (Liu et al., 2025): per-token clipped surrogate terms are summed over all completions in the batch and divided by a constant (number of completions $\times$ max_completion_length), with no per-sequence length normalization:

$$ \begin{gathered}\mathcal{L}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{NL_{\max}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{t=1}^{|y_{i}|}\ell_{i,t},\\ \ell_{i,t}=w_{i}\min\big(\rho_{i,t}A_{i},\;\bar{\rho}_{i,t}A_{i}\big)-\beta\,k_{i,t},\end{gathered} $$

(5) where $N=128$ is the number of completions in the step, $L_{\max}=64$ , $h_{i,t}=(x,y_{i,<t})$ is the prefix,

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{i,t}=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(y_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})}, $$



$$ \displaystyle\bar{\rho}_{i,t}=\operatorname{clip}(\rho_{i,t},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon), $$



$$ \displaystyle k_{i,t}=\frac{\pi_{\text{ref}}}{\pi_{\theta}}-\log\frac{\pi_{\text{ref}}}{\pi_{\theta}}-1 $$

(the per-token KL estimator TRL uses, evaluated at $y_{i,t}$ ). $w_{i}$ is TRL’s default correction for the mismatch between the vLLM sampler and the trainer’s forward pass: the ratio of the two sequence probabilities, set to zero if it exceeds 3. It was close to 1 throughout (mean 1.00). With one optimization pass per generation batch (TRL default), $\rho=1$ in value and the loss reduces to the sequence-level policy gradient $-\sum_{i}A_{i}\nabla\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}|x)$ up to a constant, plus the KL term. When $\beta=0$ no reference model is used and the KL term is dropped.

## Abstract

Using a recently-developed technique to estimate gas temperatures ( $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ ) in star-forming regions from large photometric surveys, we propose a diagram, analogous to the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram for individual stars, to probe the evolution of individual galaxies. On this $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ -sSFR (specific star formation rate) diagram, a small fraction of star-forming galaxies appear to be dominated by different feedback mechanisms than typical star-forming galaxies. These galaxies generically have younger stellar populations, lower stellar masses and increase in relative abundance towards higher redshifts, so we argue that these objects are in an earlier stage of galactic star formation. Further, Hubble observations find that these “core-forming” galaxies also exhibit distinct morphology, and that tracks on the $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ -sSFR diagram are also a morphological sequence. Thus, unlike starburst phases which can be triggered environmentally, these earliest, core-forming galaxies, appear to be a stage that typical galaxies go through early in their star formation history. We therefore argue that most galaxies first go through a core formation stage, then subsequently disk formation, and finally become quiescent.

## I Introduction

It is perhaps natural to divide the history of a typical galaxy into three phases, each dominated by different astrophysical processes. During the first phase, gravity brings the ingredients which will become a protogalaxy into close proximity. Then, a wide variety of baryonic processes assemble those ingredients into stars, a central supermassive black hole, and other components of a galaxy. Finally, for most high-mass galaxies, at some point in the past these formation processes have predominantly stopped due to processes which have not yet been conclusively determined, leaving a quiescent galaxy with a passive galactic nucleus.

However, at present only the latter two of these classes have been observed. A variety of methods [67, 40, 57] are capable of unambiguously labeling all but a small fraction of galaxies as either star-forming or quiescent in large photometric catalogs. The small fraction of galaxies with uncertain classifications often lie in the “green valley” [37, 48], considered a possible transition stage between bluer star-forming galaxies and redder quiescent ones.

Most star-forming galaxies exhibit remarkably similar growth, including tight relationships at fixed redshift between stellar mass and SFR (the star-forming main sequence; Noeske et al. 41, Peng et al. 44, Speagle et al. 54, Schreiber et al. 52), mass and metallicity [63, 50] and mass and radius [65]. If these relations are the end result of various feedback mechanisms [44], galaxies in a transition phase between initial assembly and subsequent main sequence-like evolution might not follow them. This anomalous behavior might even provide a means of identifying these galaxies.

Additional growth phases that do not follow these relations (or lie at the extremes) have been proposed or observed. Galaxies with enhanced star formation rates (SFR) are often described as starbursts, and lower-redshift populations of ultra-luminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs; Lonsdale et al. 34) may be related to starbursts. Simulations also suggest that there may be two star-forming phases, one burst-like and the other steady [60]. Although every galaxy is expected to have a steady star-forming phase and a quiescent phase, bursts are believed to be associated with mergers or other environmental factors [46], and thus not every galaxy will have one. Therefore, starbursts are not considered strong candidates as the earliest evolutionary phase of typical galaxies.

In this work, the IMF temperature ( $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ ) - specific star formation rate (sSFR) diagram, a galaxy analogue of the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram [20, 47] for stars, is introduced and used to produce galactic evolutionary tracks and identify galaxies in the earliest stages of star formation. These earliest galaxies exhibit distinctive properties and morphology, with a gradual transition towards more typical main sequence behavior indicating that this is an evolutionary sequence. In contrast to proposed burst phases, this new, core-forming phase is seemingly an early, steady star-forming state shared by all galaxies and transitions gradually into the more familiar main sequence. Furthermore, if most galaxies follow a similar evolutionary track, there will also be local and low-redshift analogues of this pre-main sequence phase.

In § II, the methodology behind measuring $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ from photometric catalogs is summarized, as well as several tests performed to validate these temperatures. The resulting $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ -sSFR diagram is developed in § III, along with the conclusion that the earliest stage of galaxy evolution should consist of a core-forming phase. Finally, these results are discussed in § IV, including additional predictions and a toy model providing a possible astrophysical interpretation.

## II Measuring Gas Temperatures from Photometric Surveys

This work relies on a recently-developed technique for inferring the temperature of gas in star-forming molecular clouds from multi-wavelength photometric surveys. It is expected that the IMF should depend upon the temperature of gas in star-forming molecular clouds [35, 32, 4, 26]. Thus, a measurement of the IMF might also provide a measurement of gas temperatures during the last major epoch of star formation.

The IMF is expected to depend not only on gas temperature, but on a complex series of interactions sensitive to metallicity, density, pressure, and environment [32]. As a result, the Galactic IMF is determined observationally rather than theoretically, despite the inherent difficulty of these observations resulting in several common approximations [49, 29, 9]. The Kroupa IMF [29] has two breakpoints, one determined by a Jeans mass-like calculation relating to the initial collapse of a cloud and the second by a similar calculation during fragmentation as the cloud collapses. With all other conditions held fixed, it is then possible to derive a family of IMFs which depends on the gas temperature in star-forming regions, $T_{SF}$ [26]:

$$ \frac{dN}{dm}\propto\begin{cases}m^{-0.3}&m<0.08M_{\odot}f(T_{SF})\\
m^{-1.3}&0.08M_{\odot}f(T_{SF})<m<0.5M_{\odot}f(T_{SF})\\
m^{-2.3}&0.5M_{\odot}f(T_{SF})<m,\\
\end{cases} $$

Although there is broad agreement that higher temperature lead to higher-mass breakpoints, the exact temperature dependence is more difficult to establish. Various studies have concluded that the break masses could scale as $f(T_{SF})\propto T_{SF}$ [21], $f(T_{SF})\propto T_{SF}^{3/2}$ [25], $f(T_{SF})\propto T_{SF}^{2}$ [26], or $f(T_{SF})\propto T_{SF}^{5/2}$ [10]. Here, we select the $T_{SF}^{2}$ dependence with the normalization set to match a Kroupa IMF at $T_{SF}=20$ K (which is the characteristic temperature of Galactic star-forming clouds) following the convention established in [26] and [53]

IMFs corresponding to a grid of gas temperatures, ranging from 10-60K, are then used to generate synthetic spectra using the Flexible Stellar Population Synthesis (FSPS) libraries [11] for use with the EAZY photometric template fitting code [7]. EAZY uses a basis of 12 templates generated as linear combinations of 560 individual models with various ages, star formation histories, metallicities, and extinction. A set of 12 basis templates is generated for each $T_{SF}$ . The best-fit reconstructed spectrum is then found for every object in the COSMOS2015 photometric catalog using each IMF, and the lowest $\chi^{2}$ across all IMFs is selected as the best fit.

Although in principle this allows an IMF determination for all $\sim 10^{6}$ COSMOS2015 galaxies, in practice this is not possible because of the strong covariances between the IMF, metallicity, and extinction [53]. Since they are not fully degenerate, given sufficient information it is possible to distinguish between, e.g., a bluer spectrum due to a top-heavier (or bottom-lighter) IMF and due to lower extinction. However, this requires high signal-to-noise measurements across multiple bands. In order to explore this, a mock dataset was constructed at a range of IMFs and observed in the COSMOS2015 filters. It was found that the gas temperature could be accurately recovered for the $\sim 10\%$ brightest objects in COSMOS2015, but that the remainder would require additional observations to determine the IMF [53]. The work here relies only on those $\sim 14\times 10^{4}$ objects, which is the cause for low statistics at $z\gtrsim 2$ .

In addition to these strong covariances, there is a complete mathematical degeneracy between the IMF and the star formation history (SFH), as an identical stellar population can be produced with different combinations of IMF and SFH. Mock datasets were used to show that the template fitting technique used here is primarily sensitive to the highest-mass break in the stellar population. For a continuous SFH, as is likely for typical star-forming galaxies, this should correspond to the highest-mass break in the IMF, and therefore can be used as an IMF and gas temperature indicator. However, in the case of rapid quenching, this break can instead come from the SFH, and a population of such objects is discussed in Steinhardt et al. [58] in connection with star formation turnoff. These uncommon objects often exhibit two local minima in the minimum $\chi^{2}(T_{SF})$ , with one minimum corresponding to the gas temperature (and lying on the main locus in the $T_{SF}-$ sSFR diagram) and the other corresponding to the break in SFH.

Finally, it is necessary to consider other effects on the IMF apart from gas temperature. A Jeans-mass like calculation is sensitive to anything which changes either gravitational or thermodynamical effects. In particular, it is expected that the IMF should be sensitive to metallicity in addition to temperature, and it is known that galactic metallicities change with redshift. Given the difficulty of constraining template fits with addition of a single-parameter family of IMFs, is it not possible to fit a multiple-parameter family of IMFs with current photometric surveys. Likely, the correct interpretation of $T_{SF}$ is instead as a combination of gas temperature, metallicity, and other parameters.

Nevertheless, there are several indications that interpreting $T_{SF}$ as gas temperature is reasonable [53]. Notably, a comparison between $T_{SF}$ and dust temperatures shows strong agreement (Fig. 1) in not only the broad qualitative trends but even quantitatively [59]. Thus, $T_{SF}$ proves a reasonable proxy for (cool) dust temperature, and if gas and dust are approximately in equilibrium, $T_{SF}$ should then indicate gas temperature in star-forming regions. The resulting change in stellar masses at $z\sim 2$ produces a picture more consistent with downsizing and quenching at lower redshifts [58]. This work, showing that an evolutionary sequence selected entirely from template fitting is also a morphological sequence, further validates that $T_{SF}$ is a meaningful astrophysical indicator.

## III The $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ -sSFR diagram

The key diagnostic developed in this work is the $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ -sSFR diagram. The specific star formation rate, or star formation rate per unit mass, is a measure of how efficiently a galaxy is turning material into new stars. The IMF temperature $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ [53, 56, 58, 59], is an estimate of the temperature in star-forming molecular clouds at the time of star formation. Thus, a diagram comparing $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ and sSFR is intended as an analogue of the Hertzsprung-Russell (H-R) diagram comparing $T$ and luminosity for individual stars.

$T_{\textrm{SF}}$ is also a measure of the Jeans mass [25] necessary for these clouds to collapse and form stars, so it should be expected that there is a relationship between sSFR and $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ . Using the recently-developed techniques described in Sneppen et al. [53], it is possible to determine this relationship for the first time, then use it as a probe of the astrophysics in star-forming galaxies.

It should be stressed that both sSFR and $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ are inferred quantities and rely on a large set of assumptions. It is well established that star formation rates (and therefore sSFR as well) are difficult to constrain in photometric template fitting [7, 13, 23, 54, 30, 66]. The addition of a new parameter to measure the shape of the IMF and thus infer $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ adds additional potential degeneracies [53]. Further, the remainder of this work asserts that the shape of the parametrized Kroupa IMF is a proxy for $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ , as based on the Jeans mass approximation, using a specific scaling out of several options, as described in § II.

Finally, this method assumes that galaxies can be described with a single, best-fit $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ , even though it is likely that molecular clouds in star-forming regions will have a range of gas temperatures. As a result, even if there is truly an underlying relationship between star formation efficiency and gas temperature, the best-fit sSFR and $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ for a galaxy containing molecular clouds in a wide range of conditions will not necessarily lie on that relation. However, as it is commonly done in constructing photometric catalogs and template fitting, it is necessary to approximate galaxies as being effectively monolithic. They are assumed to be well-characterized by a single gas temperature for most star-forming clouds and a single sSFR which describes the efficiency in all of those regions.

### III.1 Identifying Three Primary Growth Regimes

*Figure 2: The $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ -sSFR diagram, analogous to a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram for galaxies, for COSMOS2015 galaxies at $0.7<z<1.8$ showing bins with at least 10 data points. Panels are colored by the median (left) redshift; (top-right) stellar mass; and (bottom-right) age of the stellar population. Moving from top-right to bottom left, galaxies become more massive, with older stellar populations, and are more commonly observed at later times. Although no morphological information was used to produce the diagram, this is also a morphological sequence (see also Figure 4). The diagram is therefore interpreted as an evolutionary track followed by typical galaxies, with core-forming galaxies identified as the initial stage of star formation. The dashed region in the left panel indicates that the IMF cannot be recovered at $T_{\textrm{SF}}\lesssim 25$ K [53], although observational evidence (see § III.2) indicates that the IMF may be even bottom-heavier than $T_{\textrm{SF}}\sim 25$ K.*

The distribution of galaxies on the $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ -sSFR diagram (Fig. 2) exhibits a continuous locus which can be described as three different behaviors, labeled as core-forming, typical star-forming, and quiescent. At fixed redshift, these groups also comprise a mass sequence, with the lowest-mass galaxies selected as core-forming and the highest-mass as quiescent. Although two most distinctive relationships are in the high- $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ (core-forming) and low-sSFR (quiescent) tails of the distribution, the vast majority of objects in the COSMOS catalog, as the name suggests, are selected as typical star-forming.

The three groups are characterized by their different relationships between sSFR and $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ (Fig. 2):

- 1. Core-forming galaxies have a wide range of $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ , with an increase in $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ corresponding to only a small increase in sSFR.

- 2. Normal star-forming galaxies, the bulk of the population, have a relatively narrow range of both sSFR and $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ . The range is perhaps to narrow to effectively constrain the relationship, but the increase in sSFR with temperature is far sharper than for core-forming galaxies.

- 3. Quiescent galaxies have a wide range of sSFR, always lower than for star-forming galaxies, but are all nearly at identical $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ .

### III.2 Variations in the IMF Over Galactic Lifetimes

The tracks indicated on the $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ -sSFR diagram correspond to a range of different IMFs over the lifetime of a galaxy. The earliest, core-forming stages would be characterized by the bottom-lightest IMFs, with the IMF becoming progressively bottom-heavier over time. The eventual stellar population would be combination of all of these IMFs, although the most recent star formation (and thus the bottom-heaviest IMF) would dominate the observed light.

This mixture of different stellar populations might provide a possible explanation for the seemingly-conflicting combination of current observational measurements constraining galactic IMFs. Every technique has both large statistical uncertainties and potentially larger systematic uncertainties, and thus is individually inconclusive. Nevertheless, studies focusing on nearly every individual region of the stellar mass function appear to report an excess when compared with expectations taken from a Galactic IMF. Black hole merger rates from LIGO find an excess compared to predictions using a Galactic IMF, consistent with a top-heavier IMF that produced more black holes [28, 16]. Delay-time distributions for Type Ia supernovae indicate a possible excess of white dwarfs, which would indicate an intermediate-heavier IMF. Finally, spectral lines indicate an excess of low-mass stars in early-type galaxies compared with a Galactic IMF [12], a similar result to studies of the Gaia-Enceladus population believed to have been a dwarf galaxy prior to merging with the Milky Way [19].

Each of these results, in addition to probing a different stellar mass range, also probes a different time period. Thus, an evolutionary track that moves from an initial, bottom-light IMF to a progressively bottom-heavier IMF over time is potentially consistent with all of these results. The black hole-black hole merger excess in LIGO lies towards higher redshift. Similarly, the time delay measurements indicate an excess of white dwarfs formed at early times. However, early-type galaxies are observed very late in their evolutionary history, towards the bottom-left corner of the $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ -sSFR diagram.

In order to be consistent with the Conroy & van Dokkum [12] and Hallakoun & Maoz [19] results, quenching galaxies must not merely have a Galactic-like IMF; but must actually become bottom-heavy in the last stages of star formation. The gas temperature measurements presented here find a best-fit $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ of $\sim 25$ K, corresponding to an IMF that is instead slightly bottom-lighter than the Milky Way. However, we note that a comparison with mock datasets finds that this technique is primarily sensitive to bottom-light populations (Sneppen et al. 53, Fig. 13), since those produce the most distinctive shapes in rest-frame UV photometry. As the blue stars disappear, whether via aging of the stellar population or via a bottom-heavier IMF, the covariances become too strong to constrain the IMF, and the best-fit IMF by default ends up being approximately Galactic. Thus, a measurement of $T_{\textrm{SF}}=25$ K is more properly a measurement that $T_{\textrm{SF}}\lesssim 25$ K. If galaxies in the bottom-left corner of the $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ -sSFR diagram instead have $T_{\textrm{SF}}\sim 10-15$ K, which is still above the contribution from massive stars (cf. Papadopoulos 42), such an evolutionary track could produce all of the seemingly-conflicting observational results.

## IV Discussion

With the addition of a parameter corresponding to changes in the IMF due to the gas temperature in star-forming regions, it is possible to measure that gas temperature, $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ , in large photometric catalogs. An examination of the relationship between specific star-formation rate and the best-fit temperature finds three distinct behaviors. Core-forming galaxies exhibit a wide range of $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ at relatively similar sSFR. Typical star-forming galaxies exhibit a narrow range of both parameters at fixed redshift, consistent with previous studies [41, 44, 54, 52, 63, 50]. Finally, quiescent galaxies exhibit nearly constant $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ at a wide range of low sSFR. Previous studies have typically separated galaxies into star-forming and quiescent, but the core-forming branch is a new class of objects that arise from measuring $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ .

### IV.1 Core-forming Galaxies and “Blue Nuggets”

The core-forming galaxies bear strong resemblance to a population dubbed blue nuggets11 1 It is likely that some of the blue nuggets have been identified as “green pea” galaxies at $0.1<z<0.4$ [8]. Their physical properties appear to be the same, but their identification as distinct galaxies is based on their strong nebular emission observed in the SDSS r-band. most frequently found at $1<z<2$ [22, 31]. They have similarly high sSFR, which places them at the top of the star-forming main sequence, small stellar masses, young stars, little dust obscuration and compact morphologies, as seen in data [8, 22] and simulations [68, 61, 62, 31]. The increased abundance of core-forming galaxies towards $1<z<2$ also supports this comparison. However, best-fit Sérsic indices of the core-forming galaxies indicate that they are predominantly smaller versions of the typical star-forming galaxies, consistent with a bulge+disk structure with the index of $n\sim 1$ or irregular shape due to mergers (Fig. 3), rather than singular compact bulges. In fact, the $R_{20}$ radii show that the core-forming galaxies are just as diffuse in the center as the typical main-sequence galaxies are (with $n\sim 1$ ), in contract to very compact bulges in quiescent galaxies. It is perhaps worth noting that only one of $R_{20}$ , $R_{50}$ , and $R_{80}$ would be insufficient to see the entire picture, a result which appears to apply more broadly to galaxy morphological studies (cf. Mowla et al. 39).

As the morphological quantities suggest, most core-forming galaxies appear to be distinct from the population of blue nuggets. It is however possible that these galaxies are in a post-blue-nugget phase characterized by formation of a blue disk once the bulge is formed. In either case, the photometric procedure used here is effective for differentiating between the typical disk galaxies and their structurally similar smaller versions, which would otherwise be indistinguishable.

### IV.2 Interpretation as an Evolutionary Sequence

These three groups form a mass sequence at fixed redshift and display a progression in the best-fit age of their stellar populations (Fig. 2). The gradients in both parameters across galaxy populations indicate an evolutionary sequence between core-forming, normal star-forming and quiescent galaxies. In addition, there is a redshift dependence to their relative number densities: at higher redshift, there are more core-forming and fewer quiescent galaxies. This is consistent with numerous other studies finding mass downsizing (cf. Fontanot et al. 17) in galaxy evolution. It is therefore natural to consider core-forming galaxies as some sort of early star-forming phase, prior to typical star formation which is far more prevalent in photometric surveys.

### IV.3 Interpretation as Various Feedback Modes

A model of the various feedback mechanisms responsible for the star-forming main sequence is well beyond the scope of this work. Here, a toy model is proposed which might explain the two tails (core-forming and quiescent) of the distribution.

Typical Star-Forming: Several models of the main sequence invoke tight feedback between conditions in star-forming molecular clouds and high-mass (and therefore newly-formed) stars. For example, cosmic rays from the deaths of massive stars might provide the dominant heating mechanism responsible for setting gas temperatures [42], but an increase in SFR and thus higher gas temperatures would also increase the Jeans mass and eventually regulate the SFR. At fixed gas density this would produce an equilibrium solution, and as gas density declines, an attractor solution exists [55].

A variety of different mechanisms have been proposed, including gas regulation [44, 33, 43], cosmic ray feedback [42, 55], and even stochastic processes as an alternative to feedback [27]. However, it has not yet been possible to observationally determine which, if any, of these mechanisms is correct. A possible entry point would be the discovery of galaxies transitioning from their initial assembly to main sequence-like growth, before these feedback processes have had time to dominate their observed properties.

In this picture, the two tails of the distribution would then be produced by conditions which break one of these two feedback modes.

Quiescent: As sSFR declines, at some point young stars will no longer provide the dominant contribution to gas temperature. For example, given the current Galactic SFR of $\sim 1M_{\odot}/\textrm{yr}$ , molecular cloud temperatures are insensitive to small changes in SFR. Thus, the quiescent tail of the distribution would asymptotically approach a constant $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ as sSFR goes to zero. Here, $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ decouples as it is a measure of the gas temperature at the time when the stellar population is formed and not the current temperature [53, 58].

A constant $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ thus implies that by the time galaxies start to quench, contributions from star formation have already ceased to dominate gas temperatures. This would be consistent with proposed mechanisms such as strangulation [43] or gas depletion [14]. However, a different behavior would be expected if quenching were driven by major mergers or some other external event which could occur even at high sSFR.

Core-Forming: The core-forming galaxies can perhaps be explained by breaking the other feedback mode. If a galaxy has sufficiently high gas density, an increase in temperature and the corresponding Jeans mass will have negligible effect on SFR. Rather, the limiting factor might be infall rates or other effects on gas availability.

Young, massive stars would still provide the dominant source of gas heating, but the relevant equilibrium would be set by cooling mechanisms rather than by feedback limiting SFR. For example, if the predominant cooling mechanism is black-body radiation, $\textrm{sSFR}\propto T_{SF}^{4}$ , or equivalently, $T_{SF}\propto\textrm{sSFR}^{1/4}.$

### IV.4 Inside-Out Growth

This explanation for early main sequence galaxies additionally predicts that their star-forming regions must be compact. Due to the high temperatures, stars can only form in high-density regions where the increased Jeans mass does not inhibit collapse. If baryons initially are densest in the central regions of galaxies, then stars will only form in those central regions. As $T_{SF}$ decreases, lower density regions further out will be able to form stars.

Perhaps this suggests that the two star-forming phases identified here correspond to distinct regions. In their initial stages, star-forming galaxies can only form stars in central regions, even if the morphological features of a bulge may not yet be present. Thus, we observe protogalaxies to be remarkably compact [65], and observe the oldest Galactic stellar populations towards the Galactic center [2, 64]. It is for this reason that the high- $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ branch is labeled in this work as ‘core-forming’.

Once the central region has finished forming stars, no high-density regions remain and star formation rates decline, decreasing $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ . Normal star-forming galaxies, corresponding to most of the star-forming main sequence, then form stars in the lower-density disk. This is consistent with hints that the star-forming main sequence, when viewed in terms of disk mass rather than the full stellar mass, may be redshift-independent [1]. Finally, quiescent galaxies have even ceased to efficiently form disk stars.

### IV.5 Interpretation as a Morphological Sequence

This interpretation is also supported by morphological observations of COSMOS galaxies. Much of the COSMOS field is covered by Hubble observations capable of resolving galaxies along most of the $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ -sSFR diagram at $z\lesssim 1$ . Although no morphological information was used in determining best-fit parameters, producing the $T_{\textrm{SF}}$ -sSFR diagram, or using that diagram to label objects as core-forming, typical star-forming, or quiescent, these categories nevertheless exhibit distinct morphology (Figs. 3-4).
